sections.label: Inner Life
sections.description: Psychoemotional and psychospiritual wellbeing are a huge lever for health. Probably the biggest one.

sections.label: Environment
sections.description: Settings, people, work, light, noise, nature, screens, chronic stressors, and the other things a person is continually exposed to.

sections.label: Movement
sections.description: Walking, lifting weights, cardio, and staying fit.

sections.label: Food
sections.description: Food matters, but I don’t obsess over it. My approach is flexible, bioenergetic, and Peat-adjacent.

sections.label: Frontiers
sections.description: Ideas I think deserve more attention. Some I’m fairly convinced by; others I’m still trying to understand.

entries.title: A Life Worth Inhabiting
entries.summary: Psychoemotional and psychospiritual wellbeing are a huge lever for health and wellbeing. Probably the biggest one.
entries.currentTake: What do I want out of life? What makes me excited? What am I happy to spend my days doing? Life should not simply be something I suffer through. If the structure of my life is making me miserable, changing it may matter more than optimizing another physical health variable.
supportingDetails: Physical health affects how I feel, and how I feel affects my physical health.
Feeling alive is a better North Star than becoming perfectly optimized.
To the extent possible, people should have agency over how they spend their lives.

entries.title: Freedom Is Physiological
entries.summary: A life that continually feels trapped will eventually be felt by the body.
entries.currentTake: The ability to choose where I live, how I work, and how I spend my time matters greatly to me. I don’t think chronic stress can be separated from the structure of a life.
supportingDetails: When possible, change persistent stressors instead of only getting better at tolerating them.

entries.title: Chronic Stress
entries.summary: Persistent stress from work, lifestyle, environment, or a lack of agency can be a major health input.
entries.currentTake: Stress is not just a mindset problem. Sometimes the job, place, schedule, relationship, or general structure of life is the problem. When I can change a persistent stressor, that may matter more than adding another health practice.
supportingDetails: Look at what keeps creating the stress, not only how to cope with it.
People, work, noise, screens, money, freedom, and the physical environment can all matter.

entries.title: Light Is the Main Signal
entries.summary: A proper light environment is one of the highest-priority physical inputs in my health model.
entries.currentTake: I want strong natural light during the day, especially morning outdoor light. After dark, I want to reduce or eliminate artificial light and make nighttime actually dark.
supportingDetails: Get outside early when possible. Window light is not the same as being outdoors.
Bright days. Dark nights.
Reduce screens and overhead light after dark.

entries.title: Less Screen, More World
entries.summary: I would benefit from spending less time inside screens and social media feeds.
entries.currentTake: Too much time in digital environments feels like a poor use of my attention, focus, and energy. Screens and social media are fine in moderation. Spending too much of my life there probably isn’t good for me, and it generally doesn’t feel good.
supportingDetails: Put the phone somewhere else sometimes.
More time walking, talking to people, being outside, or doing nothing.

entries.title: Nature and Ground Contact
entries.summary: I would ideally spend more time outdoors, in nature, and barefoot directly on the Earth.
entries.currentTake: I believe grounding is a real phenomenon worth taking seriously. I also think nature exposes us to many things that can benefit health and feel calming or regulating, including natural light, open space, weather, plants, and direct contact with the Earth.
supportingDetails: More time in nature is useful even without reducing it to one mechanism.
I would like more regular bare-foot contact with the Earth.

entries.title: Resonance Breathing
entries.summary: 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out. About 10 minutes first thing in the morning, usually looking out an open window.
entries.currentTake: I breathe gently through my nose and keep the rhythm steady. It’s a straightforward morning practice.
supportingDetails: Gentle rather than maximal breaths.
I also consider Buteyko breathing broadly powerful and useful, especially its focus on nasal breathing, less air, and CO₂ tolerance.

entries.title: Rest and Recovery
entries.summary: Naps are great. They’re underrated.
entries.currentTake: I also use and value NuCalm and NSDR as ways to rest and recover. Quiet time and doing nothing can be useful too.
supportingDetails: NuCalm has been in my toolkit for years.
NSDR is useful when I can’t sleep or want a short reset.

entries.title: Make Night Feel Like Night
entries.summary: Sleep starts before I get into bed.
entries.currentTake: Darkness, fewer screens, cooler air, and a reasonably consistent sleep rhythm matter. I try to make nighttime actually feel like night.
supportingDetails: Keep the room dark and reduce unnecessary light after sunset.
Start with simple environmental changes before complicated sleep technology.

entries.title: Walking
entries.summary: I walk a lot. It’s probably the most reliable form of exercise in my life.
entries.currentTake: Walking gives me movement, outdoor time, daylight, and a good way to understand a place. It also helps me think.
supportingDetails: Walking is built into how I travel and explore cities.
It’s easy to do consistently.

entries.title: Lifting Weights
entries.summary: I like looking fit as well as being fit. Maintaining muscle and my physique is probably the bigger personal driver.
entries.currentTake: After fifteen years as a trainer, I still value resistance training, useful movement patterns, and gradual progression. Looking good is a legitimate reason I train.
supportingDetails: Do what you’ll consistently do.
Useful training does not need to be complicated.

entries.title: Aerobic Base + Hard Efforts
entries.summary: I’m not currently doing much structured cardio, and I think I would benefit from more.
entries.currentTake: Closer to my ideal, I’d do a couple of easier aerobic sessions and one or two harder or interval efforts each week. I’m not doing that consistently right now.
supportingDetails: Most of the easier work does not need to feel punishing.
Walking is great, but it does not replace every kind of cardio.

entries.title: Don’t Make Food Your Religion
entries.summary: Food matters, but I don’t obsess over it and I don’t think other people should either.
entries.currentTake: My approach is flexible and Peat-adjacent. I use some principles, pay attention to how food affects me, and try not to turn diet into an identity.
supportingDetails: Use principles without joining a diet tribe.
Notice what supports energy, digestion, mood, training, and enjoyment.

entries.title: Feed the Metabolism
entries.summary: My food model is broadly bioenergetic and Peat-adjacent, but it is not a strict diet.
entries.currentTake: I generally eat enough, don’t unnecessarily fear carbohydrates, get adequate protein, choose nutrient-dense foods, prefer traditional or saturated fats, and minimize heavily processed seed oils where practical. Gelatin and collagen also make sense to me.
supportingDetails: Energy, digestion, mood, sleep, appetite, and training response are useful feedback.
Calories and protein matter, but I don’t want to track them forever.
This is a working model, not a rigid Ray Peat diet.

entries.title: Biofield + Biofield Tuning
entries.summary: I take the biofield seriously. I don’t think it should be dismissed because the standard model has trouble explaining it.
entries.currentTake: Biofield Tuning gives me a practical way to work with this through sound and direct experience. I believe the phenomenon is real, even if every proposed mechanism or map is not.
supportingDetails: The experience and the explanation are separate questions.
The relationship between sound, electrical organization, memory, and physiology is very interesting to me.

entries.title: Bioelectricity + Morphogenesis
entries.summary: Living systems appear to use bioelectric networks to coordinate form, repair, and collective behavior. I think this could be extremely important.
entries.currentTake: Michael Levin’s work asks how living systems know what shape to build, what to repair, and what counts as the self. That seems like a much bigger question than what individual molecules are doing.
supportingDetails: This is a research direction, not something I currently treat as a personal practice.

entries.title: Light Biology
entries.summary: I think light is biological information, not just illumination or a way to make vitamin D.
entries.currentTake: Circadian timing is only the beginning. Wavelength, intensity, darkness, infrared light, mitochondria, and cellular water all deserve more attention.
supportingDetails: The modern indoor light environment is very different from the one humans developed in.
Established circadian effects and more speculative mechanisms should still be distinguished.

entries.title: Structured / EZ Water
entries.summary: The water in and around living structures may be doing much more than the standard hydration story suggests.
entries.currentTake: Gerald Pollack’s exclusion-zone work and the possible links between water, charge, infrared light, and biology are worth investigating. I’m interested without assuming every health claim has been proven.
supportingDetails: A laboratory finding and a whole-body health claim are not the same thing.
This connects naturally with light biology and bioelectricity.

entries.title: EMF Biology
entries.summary: I think the biological effects of our electromagnetic environment are substantially underestimated.
entries.currentTake: Human biology developed in natural electrical and magnetic conditions, not around continuous close-range wireless exposure. Distance, duration, timing, and the sleep environment are worth taking seriously without becoming paranoid about it.
supportingDetails: Simple reductions include distance, airplane mode, hardwiring, and fewer devices near sleep.
The strongest claims still need careful review.

entries.title: Biological-Conflict Models
entries.summary: I don’t consider German New Medicine or biological decoding complete systems, but I think the conventional model is incomplete too.
entries.currentTake: I think it is worth investigating whether some symptoms can be adaptive responses to conflict or overwhelming experiences. That does not mean every fixed organ-conflict map is correct.
supportingDetails: A useful question can be: what else was happening when this began?
This should not replace appropriate medical evaluation.

entries.title: Consciousness + Physiology
entries.summary: I’ve become increasingly convinced that consciousness, expectation, meaning, and physiology cannot be cleanly separated.
entries.currentTake: Placebo and nocebo effects, attention, intention, context, and reports of non-local effects suggest a stranger relationship between mind and matter than the usual story allows. I don’t think we understand the size or mechanism of those effects yet.
supportingDetails: Meaning can affect physiology without every proposed quantum explanation being correct.
I think non-local consciousness deserves serious investigation.

entries.title: Altered-State Somatic Exploration
entries.summary: Altered states have sometimes made bodily information available that I could not access in the same way through analysis.
entries.currentTake: I’m interested in the potential of altered states for somatic exploration. They can change attention, sensation, spontaneous movement, and emotional processing. That does not mean every interpretation of the experience is literally true.
supportingDetails: This is based partly on my own experience.
I don’t see it as a universal protocol or an explanation for every symptom.
